No changes are expected in the U.S. Federal Reserve's benchmark interest rate at next week's meeting. The market takes it for granted that the U.S. monetary authority will choose to leave its monetary policy unchanged, holding rates within the 3.75%–4.00% target range set following last month's hike. According to asset management experts, the rationale is twofold: the proximity of the midterm elections and the ongoing economic resilience displayed by the United States.
"The proximity of the midterm elections, along with the need to evaluate the impact that the previous rate hike has had on the market, are among the most significant arguments for postponing a decision to raise rates again in October. Consequently, even though the September U.S. inflation print came in worse than expected across both headline and core metrics, it still appears too early to confirm an upward trend. Investors believe Warsh will opt to delay any hike until December, when the market anticipates another increase in the policy rate that will lift the target range to 4.00%–4.25%," explains Cristina Gavín Moreno, Head of Fixed Income at Ibercaja Gestión.
Furthermore, as Kish Pathak, fixed-income research analyst at MFS IM, and Erik Weisman, chief economist and portfolio manager at MFS IM, recall, comments from Vice Chairs Williams and Jefferson revealed no intention to raise rates this month. Christopher Waller stated that hikes "do not necessarily have to happen at consecutive meetings," and Bowman sees no urgency to act. Finally, Warsh's remarks in Bangkok were notable for what went unsaid: he did not repeat the forceful anti-inflation message delivered at Jackson Hole.
"Data published since the last meeting supports the view that the labor market remains in good shape and that inflation is still too elevated for comfort. At the same time, Warsh has favored focusing on broader trends. A single additional month of data does little to determine whether the trend is shifting, which is why he has advocated for reducing the number of FOMC meetings. The nature of the risks confronting the economy also counsels patience. For instance, latent inflationary pressures will ease if some resolution to the war involving Iran is reached and energy prices retreat. The economy has proven resilient amid the oil crisis thanks to robust capital expenditure linked to artificial intelligence and the wealth effect generated by equities. If the recent volatility in AI-related stocks worsens, growth could lose momentum. By December, there will be more visibility on both fronts," argue the MFS IM experts.
Bank of America (BofA) economists take a more critical view of the headline U.S. economic data, acknowledging that while there are "strong arguments for raising rates, there are substantial hurdles to executing it." They maintain their forecast that the Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points, although they recognize it will be a difficult decision to implement given market developments over the past week. "September inflation, coming in well above expectations, bolsters the case for an October hike. The October decision will test Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's resolve to introduce a radical shift in the institution's forward guidance. If the Fed raises rates, fears of excessive monetary tightening could emerge; if it holds rates unchanged, markets might question its credibility," they state.
Thus, according to market experts, the primary focus of next week's meeting lies in the Fed Chair's assessment of the condition of the U.S. economy. "Even if he does not deliver formal forward guidance, he can certainly offer clues about what to expect—not so much for the remainder of this year, where the market already prices in a December hike, but looking ahead to 2027. If consumer strength persists and inflationary pressures become entrenched, that could lead to two additional hikes next year," Gavín notes.
According to Christian Scherrmann, Chief U.S. Economist at DWS, in one of his rare public appearances outside the post-FOMC press conference, the Fed Chair refrained from commenting on the monetary policy outlook. "This was widely interpreted as a signal that the Fed will maintain the status quo, likely referencing his Jackson Hole remarks prior to the last rate increase. However, other Fed officials continue to send mixed signals. For example, Governor Christopher Waller still entertains the possibility of further hikes, even as higher Treasury yields tighten financial conditions. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson advocates for patience, while Governor Michelle Bowman sees little urgency to act. Others, such as Austan Goolsbee, Beth Hammack, John Williams, and Susan Collins, worry that inflation could prove stickier than expected. This divergence of views suggests the committee itself is divided over whether policy is already restrictive enough. In any case, central bankers have become more active in recent months rather than less, contrary to what Chair Warsh suggested. We interpret this as a sign of an engaged FOMC, which in our view reinforces the institution's independence," Scherrmann emphasizes.
For François Rimeu, Senior Strategist at Crédit Mutuel AM, although he agrees with fellow analysts that forward guidance has fallen out of favor, close attention must be paid to Warsh's remarks during the ensuing press conference. "The official statement is likely to remain largely unchanged from September: solid growth, a stable labor market without wage pressures, elevated inflation, and a reaffirmed commitment to price stability. In the press conference, Chair Warsh is expected to maintain his stance of avoiding guidance on the future path of interest rates," he adds.

items.title: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan
items.summary: Prosecutors have indicted Devin Jacob Ballard for a killing that has caused outrage in Japan, local media reports.
items.content:
Image caption, Devin Jacob Ballard was stationed at Futenma Air Station
A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.
Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.
It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.
Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".
Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.
It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.
Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl.
In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl.
In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.
The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents".
People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough."

Image caption, Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy â branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" â to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

items.content:
Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in
The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike .
"The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation."
The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks.
Chair of the Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference at the William McChesney Martin Jr. Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, July 29, 2026.
Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016.
After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year.
Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up.
Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank.
What interest rate hikes mean for you and the economy
"Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements.
"This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added.
The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank.
A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again.
Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring.
Oil prices surge after Trump vows retaliation for Iranian attack
Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses.
Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%.

"I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in."
Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year.
The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said.
"We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added.
Fed holds interest rates steady as economy weathers resurgent inflation
Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions.
In a sense, that approach has worked, some economists said. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Wednesday, after the Fed issued its rate decision.
The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage, which closely tracks the 10-year Treasury yield, stands at 6.66%, its highest level in a year, Freddie Mac data on Thursday showed.
"That market-delivered tightening is why the Fed could hold," Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of data firm GLJ Research, told ABC News in a statement. "The market did the work; Warsh banked it."
A wide gap between the benchmark rate set by central bankers, the federal funds rate, and the market for Treasuries could pose challenges for policymakers, however. Investors may seek to exploit the gap, and economic tumult could result, Gerald Epstein, a professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told ABC News.
"Eventually, the Fed would need to raise interest rates," Epstein said.
Too much focus on wonky economic questions risks overlooking the political dynamic surrounding interest rate policy, some economists said.
President Donald Trump pressured Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, in an effort to reduce interest rates. The Department of Justice opened an unprecedented criminal probe into Powell, which he viewed as part and parcel of the pressure campaign. Trump has denied any involvement in the probe, which the DOJ later dropped .
Warsh has voiced support for the independence of the Fed, but he may seek to avoid rate increases even as he vows to fight inflation, especially as the political calendar barrels toward the November midterm elections, Epstein said.
"The elephant in the room is that the hawkish tone of the Fed chair is at odds with the preference of the White House for a rate cut," Brusuelas said.

items.title: Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election?
items.summary: After years of war, displacement and restrictions, Gazans ask whether Israel’s election will affect their future.
items.content:
Share Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election? on social media
Palestinians in Gaza are watching Israel’s election amid uncertainty over continued displacement, restrictions and the prospects for rebuilding their lives [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — After three years of genocidal war, Palestinians in Gaza are watching the upcoming elections in Israel with a mixture of fear and uncertainty.
Although the territory has been under a “ceasefire” since October 2025, Palestinians in Gaza continue to endure almost daily Israeli air strikes, dire living conditions, and a punishing siege that has caused shortages of basic goods.
list of 2 items list 1 of 2 Israeli elections: What are the possible outcomes?
list 2 of 2 Gaza content creator tells Al Jazeera how much her award win means
Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday to vote for their next government, in an election that has been shaped by the war on Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been strongly criticised for his handling of security before the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel. Members of his far-right government have called for a tougher line on Gaza, including the expulsion of its population.
The people of Gaza know this election will shape their future and many have been closely watching the campaign.
Mohammed Eliyan, 36, was displaced from Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza and now lives in Deir el-Balah with his five children. He hopes a change in leadership in Israel could bring relief to Palestinians who have endured repeated displacement and war.
“We follow the Israeli election to see who will win in the next phase. We hope there might be some easing for the Palestinian cause and for us, who have been displaced again,” he told Al Jazeera.
Mohammed Eliyan, displaced from Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, hopes Israel’s election will bring change and relief to Palestinians [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera] Eliyan hopes that Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military commander and Netanyahu’s main rival, will defeat the prime minister. He sees Netanyahu as more hardline and fears that if his Likud party and far-right allies win another term, it would mean more war and further displacement for Gaza’s people.
“We hope there will be changes after the election, and that someone other than Benjamin Netanyahu will win. What Netanyahu has done to the Palestinian people, before and after October 7, has not been a small thing,” he said.
But regardless of who wins, Eliyan does not expect a major shift in Israeli policy.
“They are still our enemy, and I don’t expect things to improve dramatically,” he said. “But we hope someone else might be less harsh than Netanyahu.”
He called on Israel’s next leader to end the war, prevent displacement and starvation, and ease restrictions at Gaza’s crossings.
“We want whoever leads Israel not to be hardline. End the war and let us live in peace,” he said.
Islam Salem, displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, is uncertain whether Israel’s election will bring meaningful change for Palestinians [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera] Islam Salem, 41, is displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and has three daughters. He is following Israel’s election closely and believes the result could affect Gaza’s future and the lives of his children, likely for the worse.
“Politics is our livelihood. It is connected to everything in our lives, our living conditions and even the future of our children,” he said.
But he also believes that elections primarily serve Israeli interests, so even if there are new faces in the next government, the Gaza strategy will likely remain the same.
“Israeli policy will not change in any way. Whatever they take, they consider it theirs and a political gain for them, the gains of a war they have pursued for a long time,” Islam told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Israel’s continued control of about 65 percent of Gaza’s territory inside the “Yellow Line”. He also doubts whether reconstruction will begin soon in Gaza, where more than 80 percent of buildings have been damaged, and about two-thirds of those have been completely destroyed.
“I think reconstruction will be difficult. They do not want to give others any rights. They want their rights in full, and even more,” he said.
Years of war have left Salem struggling to imagine a future beyond his harsh daily reality.
“There is no future left for us to be afraid of. We live day by day. We have no idea what will happen next, and everything we feared has already happened,” he said.
Asked what he would say to Israel’s next prime minister, he spoke of how many in Gaza are feeling.
“If only a simple person could come and talk to him and say, ‘Leave us alone. Give us some breathing space and let us breathe.’ But he would not be convinced. What can I say to him?” he said.
Hanan Abu al-Maaza, faces an uncertain future in Gaza as Palestinians consider what Israel’s election could mean for their lives [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera] Hanan Abu al-Maaza, 57, has been displaced more than 12 times during the war on Gaza. She fears Israel’s next government could bring more suffering to its people in the besieged enclave.
“We follow the election because of the fear and anxiety we are living with. We have been displaced more than 12 times, and we are afraid they will do even worse to us than before,” she said.
“We go to sleep without feeling safe, wondering what they might do to us next. The fear is still in our heads and hearts.”
Abu al-Maaza says if Netanyahu is defeated, there will be more chance that she can return to her home in Beit Lahiya.
“I hope someone else wins, so we can have peace of mind and feel safe, and return to our homes. That is what we wish for,” she said.
After years of destruction in Gaza, she hopes Israel’s next leader will show Palestinians more mercy.
“Maybe he will say that there is nothing left in Gaza, that they have done enough and should let people live. There is hardly anything left in Gaza for anyone to think about doing anything more,” she said.
Abu al-Maaza urged Israel’s next leader to end the war and stop the suffering in the territory.
“We have had enough of war and destruction. There is nothing left to destroy, yet the suffering continues,” she said.
Manar Owaida, displaced from northern Gaza, follows Israel’s election closely amid uncertainty over what its outcome could mean for Palestinians [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera] Manar Owaida, 23, is originally from northern Gaza and is now displaced in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City. She is also keeping an eye on the Israeli election and considering its potential impact.
“I follow the election to know what they are saying and planning, and to understand what is happening around us and how the next Israeli government might affect the situation in Gaza,” she said.
Owaida hopes Gadi Eisenkot will replace Netanyahu, and sees the current prime minister as more extreme than his challenger. But she does not believe a change in Israel’s leadership would transform Palestinian lives, arguing that government policies have remained consistent for decades.
“Israel’s policy is one of crime, killing and destruction. Since 1948, it has been the same policy, the same killing and the same blockade,” she said.
Still, she hopes a new government could ease restrictions and killings and withdraw from areas beyond the “Yellow Line”, allowing life to gradually return to Gaza.
“There might be a change in Israeli policy if someone comes in place of Netanyahu and eases the blockade and the killing we are living through,” she said.
“There could be a withdrawal from the Yellow Line and life could gradually return to Gaza. But we are waiting with fear and uncertainty, alongside a little hope.”
Her greatest concern is that Netanyahu could launch a wider regional war to avoid domestic political pressure around the time of the vote.
Owaida said she wants Israel’s next prime minister to allow Palestinians to live without fear of further violence.
“We want to live in freedom and peace, away from killing and wars,” she said.
Mousa Ali, a father of four, now lives in Gaza City after being displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera] Mousa Ali, 33, was displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and is now in Gaza City with his four children.
He believes that the outcome of the election could determine whether displaced Palestinians can return to areas beyond the “Yellow Line”.
“For Palestinians, this election is critical, especially because of the Yellow Line. We hope the opposition will be better when it comes to allowing displaced people to return to their areas,” he said.
Ali mentioned Gadi Eisenkot as a possible alternative and hopes Arab parties will perform strongly so they have a role in the next government.
But he does not expect a new leader to bring major changes for the people of Gaza and fears that Israeli attacks will continue. He says a Netanyahu victory would prolong displacement and control over areas around the “Yellow Line”.
“Every day in Gaza, there is blood, there are people being killed, and there is bombing everywhere,” he said. “We hope this policy will end and that a new prime minister will stop this ongoing bloodshed.”

items.content:
More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA
More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA
NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November, says BMA
Industrial action by senior doctors to begin on 25 November with only emergency cover provided, union says
England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their pay and hours, prompting NHS bosses to warn that patients will suffer “pain, discomfort and inconvenience”.
Consultant doctors, who currently earn an average of £152,000 a year, will stage a two-day walkout on 25 and 26 November, as hospitals gear up for the extra pressures winter brings.
On those days, hospitals will operate with consultants providing only emergency cover, in the way they do on Christmas Day, because most will withdraw their labour.
Consultants decided to strike after 18 months of talks with the government did not lead to agreement on key issues, including their call for action to address a 25% fall in the real-terms value of their salaries since 2009-10, the British Medical Association (BMA) said.
The senior doctors also want a 10% cut in their working hours so that, for example, a consultant working a 40-hour week would see that shrink to 36 hours.
The BMA accused ministers of “ignoring” consultants’ concerns about burnout related to their workloads and said last week’s well-below-inflation pay offer of a 2.4% increase for next year was the last straw.
Consultants voted in July to take industrial action. The BMA said that since then, informal talks with the Department of Health and Social Care had produced no “meaningful” progress, only another cut to the value of their pay.
Consultant doctors last went on strike in 2023, when they walked out for nine days. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Ciarán Devane, the head of the NHS Alliance, which represents NHS leaders, said he was “astonished and dismayed” by the BMA’s move at a time when the health service was working to tackle a backlog of more than 6 million patients awaiting more than 7m treatments.
“NHS leaders will be both astonished and dismayed by the BMA’s decision to proceed with walkouts by consultants at a time when plans to restore waiting time targets hang by a thread and as teams make wider preparations for winter after a gruelling summer,” Devane said. “Any decision to down tools risks throwing these plans further off course and will once again disrupt patient care while severely hitting NHS finances.
“A consultant walkout will result in non-urgent outpatient appointments, elective surgeries and follow-ups being postponed or rescheduled. While [postponement] is needed in the interests of patient safety, it will potentially leave patients in unnecessary pain, discomfort, and inconvenience.”
The BMA’s decision presents the prime minister, Andy Burnham, with a considerable challenge as he grapples with tight public finances and Labour’s aim of improving access to NHS care.
In June, resident doctors – formerly known as junior doctors – accepted a deal to end a campaign of strikes that had lasted more than three years. Consultants last staged stoppages in 2023, when they walked out for nine days during four strikes.
“Since we entered into dispute over 18 months ago we have engaged in good faith with the government, proposing practical solutions,” said Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, the co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee. “But time and time again ministers have kicked the can down the road. Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.
“Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough.
“Not only is our pay still a quarter down in real terms on what it was 17 years ago, having fallen more steeply than the rest of the economy, but we are also not being given time to dedicate our all to the NHS and patients, with quality and improvement being traded for the treadmill of target-chasing, driving colleagues to burnout through excessive workloads.”
Ben Morrin, the chief executive of NHS Employers, which represents England’s 205 health trusts, urged the BMA to be realistic about what size of pay rise was affordable.
“We need to be honest and transparent about what the NHS can afford at this time. If that limit is reached and industrial action takes place, we owe it to patients to focus on delivering the safest care we can,” he said.
He added that the strike would “weaken the clinical teams in every NHS hospital, which are essential to delivering high-quality patient care this winter”.

Brexit deal is not good enough for British public, says Andy Burnham
EU exit has damaged economy and failed to bring promised benefits, says PM, but he rules out big pre-election changes
Brexit has not “played out” like it was promised to the public, has weakened the economy and the current deal is not good enough, Andy Burnham has said, while ruling out any major changes in the current parliament.
The prime minister said Britain had ended up with a “harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign” and it had not helped to control the small boats crisis. Backing the home secretary’s tougher immigration rules , he said Brexit had weakened the UK’s ability to control its borders as it could no longer send people back to Europe.
When asked directly on Monday whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, Burnham told Good Morning Britain: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”
Explaining why he even brought up the possibility of “going all the way” in terms of closer relations with the EU, Burnham said: “Looking back at Brexit … I don’t think it has played out as people said it would at the time. We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign.
“It’s weakened our economy. It’s also weakened our control of immigration, and that might surprise people because that was the big issue, but the small boats crisis has risen since and we have a different form of immigration now.”
He added: “I am not going to say at the moment that the deal we’ve got is good enough for Britain. I don’t think it is good enough.”
Burnham said he would not “move away from the red lines in Labour’s manifesto”, adding: “I’m not proposing rejoining [the EU] in this parliament. We’re way, way away from that at this particular point in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better.”
There are concerns among Labour MPs who represent leave-voting constituencies in the north of the England and the Midlands that reopening the Brexit debate could create opportunities for Reform UK.
Asked about the fact that 65% of his constituents in Makerfield voted to leave the EU, the prime minister said: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing. The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit … What I can do though is make practical steps to make the arrangements work better.”
Emphasising the negative impact Brexit had had on Britain’s control of immigration, the Labour leader said: “I think we’ve got weaker control now. The reason the small boats crisis has arisen is because we can’t return people, and people know we can’t do that in the same way that we used to be able to.”
Burnham said he hoped the UK-EU summit on 20 November could yield a deal “which would be good for British food manufacturers, because they’ve been hit hard by Brexit”.
He said he backed “the principle” of the home secretary’s controversial plan to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
Burnham said Shabana Mahmood was right to pursue the plans based on the principle that “settlement is a right to be earned not just something that is granted automatically”.
He also ruled out calling an early general election, despite polling suggesting Labour was still enjoying a “Burnham bounce” . “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.”
On Wednesday’s budget, Burnham said it would offer people and businesses “breathing space”, claiming it would give Britain “a little bit of light at the end of the tunnel”.

In Egypt, Guterres warns against Iran-US escalation
Peace and Security UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for dialogue and diplomacy to end the war between Iran and the United States in remarks on Monday to journalists in Cairo, Egypt.
“ I want to send a loud and clear message to the parties. We need maximum restraint and diplomatic solutions ,” he said.
“If the sabre-rattling we are witnessing now translates itself into a major escalation, the situation in the region can get out of control.”
Moreover, navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea – critical maritime corridors for global trade.
He commended Egypt for its mediation role in helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the sides.
The Secretary-General was speaking alongside Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty following meetings focused on this and other crises in the Middle East and Africa.
“Egypt is a pillar of multilateralism,” he said. “And at a time when divisions are deepening, it is critical to keep the channels of diplomacy open .”
On Gaza, Mr. Guterres expressed profound appreciation for Egypt’s indispensable role, noting that the country has been central to mediation and humanitarian efforts since the beginning of the conflict .
He commended continued support in facilitating life-saving aid, medical evacuations and the work of humanitarian partners such as the Egyptian Red Crescent.
The Secretary-General called for Israeli restrictions on humanitarian assistance to be lifted and obstacles blocking implementation of the UN Security Council -endorsed comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict to be removed.
“Civilians must be protected and international law must be respected,” he said.
The UN chief said he was also deeply alarmed by Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank, pointing to expanding settlements, “unrelenting” evictions, surging violence, assaults, and attacks against journalists and diplomats.
“ We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment with the spectre of ethnic cleansing looming ever larger. This must end ,” he said.
Moreover, there can be no durable peace in the Middle East without the realization of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination, he said, once again upholding the two-State solution.
The Secretary-General also addressed the war in Sudan. He said that “the fighting must stop”, adding that the country’s future “must belong to the Sudanese people through an inclusive pro-political process that preserves its unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity”.
Regarding Libya, he said that “it is time to build on political momentum, unify institutions and pave the way for national elections, finally bringing the prolonged transition to an end.”
The UN chief leaves office at the end of the year and this marked his ninth visit to Egypt since being appointed in 2017.
Mr. Guterres began his remarks by explaining that he has come back repeatedly “because when this region and our world have faced some of the most difficult moments, Egypt has consistently worked to open space for diplomacy ”.

items.content:
Tulane political science professors discuss Iran war, international policy
The Tulane Journal of Policy and Political Economy hosted a panel of Tulane University professors to discuss the 2026 Iran war last Thursday.
Christopher Fettweis, an associate professor of political science, began the panel by discussing the Twelve-Day War that occurred in June 2025 between Iran and Israel.
“The Iranians were nowhere near nuclear weapons when this war started,” Fettweis said. “Iranian nuclear weapons wouldn’t have been that scary. At least not as scary as your imagination may take it to be.”
Fettweis explained the possibilities of Iranian nuclear capabilities and claimed Iran would have no purpose to use nuclear weapons if they possessed them.
“It's crazy to think that we needed to use violence to go to war to prevent the Iranians from getting nuclear weapons,” Fettweis said. “If they got them … it would be bad, but it really wouldn't be the end of the world.”
Christina Kiel, a senior professor of practice in political science, examined how international policy helped develop the conflict.
Iran signed the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action in 2015 with several world powers, including the United States. The agreement severely restricted Iran’s nuclear program.
“Iran allowed inspectors access to any site anywhere in the country they seem suspicious of, which is quite extraordinary for sovereign countries,” Kiel said. “By 2018, the U.S. withdrew from [the deal] and started this maximum pressure campaign instead, stating that this is a bad deal and we need something else.”
Andrew Leber, an assistant professor of political science, explained the economic fallout from the conflict.
“[The war] has profound economic consequences by closing the Strait of Hormuz, which is a major artery of energy flows,” Leber said. “Oil is coming up at a much higher cost, which you have probably noticed if you drive a car.”
“Many other things that people didn't realize came from the Gulf. A lot of fertilizers are produced in the Gulf,” he said. “That's part of why your food is getting more expensive in the grocery store.”
Leber also mentioned how the conflict affects other groups in the region.
“When you have one country like Iran trying to close the Strait of Hormuz for economic geopolitical leverage, there are other armed factions like Mansara or the Houthis in Yemen, who are linked to Iran in a complicated way,” he said. “We've seen this kind of cat and mouse between other countries in the region, like Saudi Arabia, finding new ways to get oil out, and other factions finding new ways to shut those supply lines down.”

The Ballon d'Or winner will be announced in London on 26 October - but who is going to win it?
Bookmakers have Spain winger Lamine Yamal and England captain Harry Kane very close together as clear favourites.
Lamine Yamal won La Liga with Barcelona and the World Cup with Spain, while Kane scored 73 goals for German champions Bayern Munich and England.
Eight-time winner Lionel Messi, of Argentina and Inter Miami, and Real Madrid's France forward Kylian Mbappe are the other probable candidates.
Or how about one of Paris St-Germain's back-to-back European champions?
BBC Sport asked several of its football experts who they think should take home the award.

European football expert Guillem Balague: Can you imagine this Ballon d'Or not won by a PSG player or a Spanish player? Impossible. So gone is Kylian Mbappe.
The PSG players, there are so many of them that deserve it - Fabian Ruiz, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Ousmane Dembele, Vitinha. So the vote is going to be split.
There is only one Spaniard who deserves it, and that's Lamine Yamal, who has given us individual performances, collective trophies, and has that aura. He's going to win it.
Image caption, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is a two-time Champions League winner with PSG
European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one.
He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup.
He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.
Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock : I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.
BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him.
Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.
Image caption, Harry Kane scored six goals at the 2026 World Cup for England
Former England striker Alan Shearer: The winner of the Ballon d'Or should be Harry Kane. His numbers for the last 12 to 18 months have been absolutely sensational for Bayern and for England. For that reason, he should get it.
Ex-England midfielder Danny Murphy: My choice for the Ballon d'Or is Harry Kane. I think his goalscoring has been relentless, brilliant. He's had one of the best seasons of his career and it'll be a great reward for him if he gets the trophy. He's been brilliant at Bayern Munich since he's been there, adapted really well and he's been the best centre-forward in the world for the last 12 months.
Former Tottenham and Crystal Palace forward Andros Townsend : Harry Kane should win the Ballon d'Or. He scored 73 goals in 65 games, 36 of those in the Bundesliga. He led Bayern Munich to the league and cup double. He scored 14 goals in the Champions League, helping Bayern Munich to the semi-finals and scored six goals in the World Cup, leading England to the semi-finals. He has had an outstanding year.
Figure caption, Why Kane deserves to win the Ballon d'Or
Former England striker Ellen White : It's a tough one but I'll go with my heart - I'd love to see Harry Kane win it. I know he didn't win the World Cup but his numbers are absolutely extraordinary, with what he has achieved with Bayern Munich and England. Lamine Yamal had a few injuries but I know he won the World Cup and I'm sure he will win the Ballon d'Or one day. Michael Olise has also been phenomenal.
Norwegian football journalist Lars Sivertsen on Champions League Match of the Day: I would like to see Harry Kane win it, he deserves it. He is a real leader at Bayern Munich. He never makes trouble and is a role model. But I do wonder if him being a low-key character hurts him. The Ballon d'Or is a popularity contest. I love that he doesn't do all that but maybe he should.

Upstream oil and gas news for exploration and production professionals
1947 Oil & Gas , the newly formed oil and gas production company focused on aggregating and redeveloping assets in the United States Gulf Coast and Gulf of America, has announced several operating updates since its listing on the London Stock Exchange's AIM market and closing its transaction with Renaissance Offshore, LLC.
At the Eugene Island 331 Field production was restored in late September 2026, following an extended shut-in period due to repairs in a downstream condensate gathering facility. Production was restored at a rate of 1,200 barrels of oil equivalent ("boepd") gross and approximately 1,000 boepd net, which is 81% oil weighted.
Further, a production increase was seen in the Ship Shoal 198 field due to a recent workover campaign prior to closing the Renaissance transaction at the end of September 2026. Production of this asset has increased to 1,275 boepd gross, 1,060 boepd net, after averaging 545 boepd net in the first half of 2026.
Additionally, the Company has been awarded two offshore lease blocks by the Marine Minerals Administration ("MMA") as part of the Big Beautiful Gulf 3 Lease Sale which took place on 12 August 2026. This is the third offshore oil and gas lease sale in the Gulf of America required under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act established to advance responsible redevelopment of the USA's offshore energy resources.
The two blocks awarded are West Delta 133 and South Timbalier 314 in the Gulf of America, which will add 10,000 gross acres to the portfolio, increasing 1947's acreage under lease. The two lease blocks were previously in the Renaissance portfolio; however, both leases now carry a lower 12.5% royalty rate, which will improve the economics in the re-development opportunities available to the company. The bid for the two lease blocks totalled approximately $260,000.
Tim Duncan, Executive Chairman of 1947 commented ; "We are excited to have Eugene Island 331 back on-line and the increase in production at the Ship Shoal 198 field, both in-line with our expectations. This will ensure a positive end to 2026 as we look forward to more catalysts in 2027. Since closing the Renaissance transaction, the Company is high-grading organic opportunities internally while continuing to look at market opportunities externally and we are excited about our path forward in being a reliable consolidator and counterparty of choice for the Basin."
1947 aims to build a leading independent producer, through the roll-up of mature conventional oil-weighted assets that benefit from new technology and new investment, specifically in the Gulf of America and along the US Gulf Coast. The Company was founded by Jeff Currie and Ivan Murphy and is led by Executive Chairman, Tim Duncan.

SpaceX's Elon Musk reveals $40 billion in debt for AI chips, warns of neoclouds
SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk said his company closed on $40 billion in financing to pay for specialized chips used to power AI, but warned that access to debt is drying up for companies that solely rely on data center revenue.
"As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," wrote Musk on X on Sunday.
Musk went on to say that SpaceX ( SPCX ) closed $40 billion in debt for Nvidia's ( NVDA ) GPUS or graphics processing units used for AI, but highlighted that the space company is "investment-grade" and has Starlink & rocket launch revenue.
In a follow-up post, Musk noted this "is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2. Not a major factor this quarter."
Musk's comments reignited concerns about the rising cost of capital and the business models of so-called neoclouds, which rent computing power to train and run AI models.
The debt disclosure comes on the heels of SpaceX's better-than-expected quarter.
The company's AI segment brought in $7.6 billion in the third quarter, more than Starlink and the rocket business combined, and more than half of SpaceX's $14.6 billion in total revenue.
Musk also took a shot at neoclouds, companies that rent out computing power and AI chips, saying they are "going to see guppy-level death and consolidation."
"Some will make it through, but not many," said Musk.
Shares of neocloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) sank more than 3% in pre-market.
The comments following a viral chart earlier this month highlighted CoreWeave's spiking bond yields, underscoring concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet.
CoreWeave shares have tanked more than 37% over the past month.

US Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Futures Edge Higher On Fed Inflation Crossroads
The Morning Bull - US Market Morning Update Monday, Oct, 26 2026
US stocks are set for a cautiously positive open, with sentiment driven less by overseas moves and more by a single question: Can the Federal Reserve ignore stubborn inflation expectations when growth data still look strong?
The University of Michigan survey pegs year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.7% in October 2026, a five-month high. At the same time, the US Composite PMI sits at 57.6, pointing to firm business activity and resilient demand.
That mix of sticky inflation views and solid output keeps pressure on borrowing costs. Higher expected policy rates can filter into corporate funding costs, squeeze interest-sensitive business models, and narrow the cushion in earnings estimates if pricing power weakens.
The unresolved issue is how the Fed weighs that 4.7% inflation outlook against strong PMIs when it meets next week. Either growth or prices will need to blink first, and current positioning in US equities reflects that policy fork in the road.
Microsoft heads into a busy earnings week under a spotlight, as traders question when heavy AI spending will feed through to profits. Management has reorganized reporting into Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer, and is pitching AI agents like Microsoft 365 Copilot and its Maia 300 chip as the payoff. Watch management's detail on AI costs and revenue traction.
SWI Compute has come out of stealth with plans to build NVIDIA powered AI factories in Europe, starting with a 30 MW facility in the UK. It has placed about US$1b in NVIDIA hardware orders and lined up initial client contracts. This adds another datapoint on demand for NVIDIA chips tied to large scale AI infrastructure build outs.
Coinbase Global shares are down 2.7% as the company expands its reach in payments through a new partnership with Thunes. The deal pipes USDC infrastructure into Thunes' network so businesses can send stablecoin payouts that land as local fiat in bank accounts or mobile wallets. Upcoming earnings will show how far these products and other new lines are gaining traction.
Venture Global (VG) surged 9.29% as traders linked the LNG producer to renewed focus on long term export contracts.
Crown Castle (CCI) jumped 9.06% after reports of advanced talks with SpaceX over leasing tens of thousands of cell towers.
CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) gained 8.25% as cybersecurity stocks rallied following warnings about critical PHP flaws and potential increased remediation work.
Bloom Energy (BE) fell 11.24% after an earnings beat, raised guidance, and negative free cash flow concerned investors.
Credo Technology Group Holding (CRDO) declined 9.51% after MaxLinear targeted its core active electrical cable market with competing chips.
Comfort Systems USA (FIX) dropped 9.26% after strong Q3 results led to profit taking and concern over margin pressure and a CFO transition.
US trading is lining up around a tight cluster of Fed decisions, inflation data and heavyweight earnings that all speak directly to how long borrowing costs stay restrictive.
Fed Interest Rate Decision , Wed 28 Oct. The policy rate currently at 4% sits against Michigan inflation expectations of 4.7%, so any hint the Fed is less patient on prices could lift Treasury yields and pressure rate sensitive stocks.
US Core PCE Price Index MoM , Thu 29 Oct. Economists look for a 0.3% print after 0.2%. A softer number would ease pressure on the Fed path and the dollar, while anything above 0.3% keeps higher funding costs in play for longer.
US GDP Growth Rate QoQ Adv , Thu 29 Oct. Consensus is 3.2% after 2.2%. A result below 3.2% would sit awkwardly with the strong 57.6 Composite PMI and could cool enthusiasm for economically sensitive sectors even if it helps rate expectations.
US Employment Cost Index QoQ , Fri 30 Oct. Markets expect 0.8% after 0.9%. A reading above 0.8% would underline persistent wage pressure, which can keep services inflation sticky and reduce scope for lower borrowing costs.
Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet earnings , Wed 28 Oct. With both reporting Q3 results after the close, commentary on AI infrastructure spending versus monetisation will influence how investors think about cash generation and capital intensity across large cap US tech.
Tech has slipped over the past week and month while still showing strong year to date and 1 year gains. Big AI projects at Microsoft, Amazon and others require heavy data center and chip spending, which feels more uncomfortable when Fed rate expectations creep higher and borrowing stays expensive.
If you hold broad US tech funds, the key swing factor is this Wednesday's Fed interest rate decision because any change in tone on inflation can quickly move rate sensitive growth sectors.
Semiconductors : Strong year, funding questions building
Semiconductors remain well ahead over the past year, yet the last 7 days show a clear step back after a sharp 30 day slide. Comments from Nvidia on intense GPU demand sit next to warnings that funding for pure AI cloud operators is drying up, which makes investors ask how much of the current chip cycle relies on easy capital.
For portfolios that lean on chip stocks or ETFs, focus on Thursday's US Core PCE inflation report since a firmer reading can keep yields elevated and pressure interest rate sensitive hardware names.
Energy & Oil and Gas : Cash flow story still in focus
Energy and Oil and Gas are both up over the past week and month on top of very strong 1 year gains. US producers and pipeline operators continue to benefit from firm commodity pricing and export projects, while incidents like Borr Drilling's rig loss highlight operational risk that can tighten supply pockets.
If you own energy producers or midstream funds, the data point that matters most near term is next week's EIA crude inventory release because signs of tighter US stockpiles often feed quickly into earnings expectations for this group.
Real Estate has risen over the last 7 days but is only slightly higher over the past month, which lines up with brief rallies against still restrictive borrowing costs. REITs tied to apartments and commercial property, such as UDR, are seeing selective analyst optimism, yet elevated mortgage rates and soft consumer sentiment keep a lid on enthusiasm.
For anyone holding REITs or housing linked ETFs, Tuesday's US building permits and new home sales numbers are the release to watch because they give a clean read on how higher rates are feeding into actual construction and transaction volumes.
Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals & Biotech : Trial wins support defensive appeal
Healthcare and Pharmaceuticals & Biotech are both positive across 7 day, 30 day and 1 year periods. A run of encouraging oncology and immunotherapy trial updates from companies like Johnson & Johnson, Regeneron and Agenus, plus ongoing pipeline news, keeps attention on drug development rather than day to day swings in consumer demand.
If you use this sector as a stabiliser, the main macro catalyst is Thursday's US GDP and PCE inflation pack since a mix of firm growth and sticky prices can keep interest in earnings streams that feel less tied to discretionary spending.
